As the artificial intelligence boom matures, choosing between high-growth processors and steady analog chips requires a careful look at Advanced Micro Devices (AMD +2.95%) and Texas Instruments (TXN +4.44%) as potential long-term investments.
Advanced Micro Devices focuses on high-performance computing for data centers and gaming, while Texas Instruments dominates the analog world with chips for industrial and automotive uses. While both operate in the same broad category, their business models and growth profiles offer very different opportunities for retail investors today.
Advanced Micro Devices designs processors and graphics chips for everything from laptops to massive data centers. Key partnerships include a strategic agreement with OpenAI to deploy advanced graphics units, alongside long-term deals with Sony (SONY +1.41%) and Microsoft (MSFT +0.92%) for gaming hardware. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business since a few large buyers drive much of the volume.
In fiscal 2025, revenue reached nearly $34.6 billion, an increase of 34% over the prior year. Net income was roughly $4.3 billion, and AMD reported a net margin of approximately 12.5% for the year. This upward trend highlights the strong demand for the company's newest products among semiconductor stocks.
As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is approximately 0.1, indicating that AMD relies very little on borrowed money. The current ratio, which measures a company's ability to pay short-term debts with current assets, is roughly 2.9. Free cash flow reached nearly $6.7 billion, though note that stock-based compensation represented roughly 21.2% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.
Texas Instruments offers a massive catalog of more than 80,000 products, focusing on analog and embedded processing. The company serves over 100,000 customers globally, primarily in the industrial and automotive markets. Because the customer base is highly diverse, with roughly half of total revenue generated by customers outside of its largest 50, the company does not rely heavily on any single buyer.
In fiscal 2025, revenue reached nearly $17.7 billion, up 13% compared to the previous year. Net income was $5 billion, resulting in a net margin of roughly 28%. In its latest annual report, filed for the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, Texas Instruments highlighted its focus on making electronics more affordable through its manufacturing scale.
Based on the December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is close to 0.9. The current ratio is approximately 4.4, suggesting the company maintains a strong cushion for its immediate financial obligations. Free cash flow for the year was nearly $2.6 billion, providing capital to support its long-term manufacturing expansion and return value to shareholders.
Advanced Micro Devices faces intense competition from Intel (INTC -0.56%) and Nvidia (NVDA +1.34%), especially following strategic partnerships between those rivals. Geopolitical risks are also present, as U.S. export controls on advanced chips to China have caused inventory charges. Additionally, the company relies heavily on TSMC (TSM +2.96%) for manufacturing and must navigate the integration of recent acquisitions like ZT Systems.
Texas Instruments must manage the cyclical nature of the chip industry, which often sees volatile demand. Because the company owns its manufacturing plants, it faces high fixed costs that are difficult to reduce during market downturns. Significant revenue comes from customers in China, making it vulnerable to trade barriers. TI is also currently in the middle of acquiring Silicon Laboratories (SLAB +0.11%).
Advanced Micro Devices trades at a significantly higher premium than Texas Instruments when comparing the forward P/E and P/S ratio metrics.

Which stock would I buy in 2026?
Presumably, investors are paying a premium for AMD because of its strong revenue growth (Texas Instruments' growth didn't come close to AMD's last fiscal year). That said, I am more interested in each company's net margin. Using fiscal 2025 figures, TI's margin pretty handily tops AMD's full-year results. And while both companies have seen profits expand by a few percentage points over the trailing 12 months, that profitability gap has continued into this fiscal year.
As far as their actual business models, I do think AMD's fabless approach is more attractive, because it gives the company more flexibility. Texas Instruments, conversely, has to deal with the high fixed costs of owning and running its manufacturing plants.
AMD stock has absolutely exploded over the past 10 years, while Texas Instruments shares have modestly outperformed the S&P 500 over that same time frame. Past performance is no indication of future results, but it's worth taking into consideration.
All told, I like Texas Instruments better here because it appeals to the conservative side of me: It’s not crazy expensive, it has stronger profitability, and it pays a dividend yielding just over 2.1%.

Texas Instruments and Infineon Technologies have upgraded to Platinum membership in the Zephyr Project, deepening their investment in the open source RTOS and its developer community.
These increased commitments provide additional resources for Zephyr's technical development, infrastructure and community programs.
The announcement coincides with the Zephyr Developer Summit (Oct. 7-9) and Zephyr Maintainers Forum (Oct. 6) in Prague, where the community marks Zephyr's 10th anniversary with more than 40 technical sessions, over 45 speakers and the first-ever Zephyr Community Awards.
PRAGUE, Oct. 1, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Zephyr Developer Summit – The Zephyr® Project, an open source project at the Linux Foundation building a secure, connected and flexible real-time operating system (RTOS) for resource-constrained devices, today announced that Texas Instruments (TI) and Infineon Technologies have upgraded to Platinum membership. Announced ahead of the Zephyr Developer Summit, co-located with Open Source Summit Europe, the expanded commitments from two leading semiconductor companies reinforce growing industry investment in Zephyr as a vendor-neutral, open source foundation for embedded development.
TI and Infineon bring longstanding technical relationships with the Zephyr community. TI has contributed to the project since its inception in 2016, providing software and board support while integrating Zephyr across its embedded portfolio. Infineon is also an active contributor and supports Zephyr across multiple embedded platforms. The move to Platinum membership will provide additional resources for the project's technical development, infrastructure and community programs.
"Ten years ago, Zephyr set out to give the embedded industry a common open source RTOS that companies could build on together," said Kate Stewart, Vice President of Dependable Embedded Systems at the Linux Foundation. "Seeing two major semiconductor companies that have contributed to Zephyr for years increase their participation is a strong sign of how far that model has come. This support gives the community more resources and makes Zephyr available to more developers building embedded products."
Since its launch, Zephyr has grown into a global ecosystem spanning a broad range of architectures, boards and embedded applications. As open source plays a growing role in embedded development, Zephyr provides a common platform where semiconductor companies, developers and product manufacturers can collaborate on shared technology. The increased engagement from TI and Infineon will help Zephyr advance its technology, hardware ecosystem and developer community as it enters its second decade.
"As a platinum-level member, Infineon is expanding its investment in the Zephyr community to help developers bring connected, resource-constrained devices to market more efficiently," said Clark Jarvis, Zephyr Governing Board Representative at Infineon. "Building on a decade of Zephyr innovation, we are committed to enabling greater software reuse and portability across our microcontroller (MCU), automotive MCU, and connectivity portfolios. This deeper engagement reflects our ambition to deliver an even better developer experience, strengthen security, and broaden hardware support throughout the Zephyr ecosystem."
"TI is committed to breaking down the barriers between hardware and software through continuous innovation. The Zephyr Project is a cornerstone of that effort," said Marian Kost, vice president and general manager of Wireless Connectivity at TI. "We are continuing our investment in open-source software and the developer community. TI wants to ensure that everyone – from a hobbyist to an engineer – can accelerate their path from concept to commercial product."
The upgraded memberships come as the Zephyr community gathers in Prague at Open Source Summit Europe to continue celebrating the project's tenth anniversary. The week opens with the Zephyr Maintainers Forum on Oct. 6, a working session where maintainers, Technical Steering Committee members and subsystem owners set the project's technical direction on release planning, security and safety support, and cross-subsystem coordination. It is followed by the Zephyr Developer Summit on Oct. 7-9, featuring more than 40 technical sessions from over 45 speakers across functional safety, security and CRA readiness, connectivity, developer tooling and testing, and real-world use cases in automotive, space and industrial applications. The summit also hosts the Zephyr Community Awards on Oct. 7, recognizing standout contributors from across the ecosystem for their work and support over the last decade.
Check out the complete Zephyr Developer Summit schedule or to learn more about the Zephyr Project and how to participate, visit zephyrproject.org.

MCHP Expands Ethernet Portfolio: Can it Challenge TXN & ADI?
Thu, October 1, 2026 at 6:20 AM PDT 4 min read
Microchip Technology MCHP has expanded its 10BASE-T1S Single Pair Ethernet portfolio with the launch of the LAN8679 and LAN8680 PMD transceivers and the LAN8660X/1X/2X endpoint family with integrated transceivers. The products are designed for next-generation zonal architectures across automotive, industrial, robotics and aerospace and defense applications, extending Ethernet connectivity to edge nodes while reducing wiring and system complexity. The portfolio combines transceivers, endpoint functionality, power management and embedded-control capabilities, thereby supporting MCHP's broader Total System Solutions strategy. It also improves competitive prowess against the likes of Texas Instruments TXN and Analog Devices ADI.
The LAN8679 features an Open Alliance 3-Pin interface in a compact package, while the LAN8680 adds power management, wake as well as sleep control and watchdog supervision. The LAN8660X/1X/2X family integrates a transceiver into a single-chip Remote Control Protocol solution, eliminating the need for external PHY components in applications such as control systems, lighting and audio. Microchip's 10BASE-T1S multidrop architecture can connect eight or more nodes over a single bus, helping reduce wiring weight, costs and gateway requirements.
The portfolio expansion strengthens Microchip's connectivity and networking growth strategy. The company identifies connectivity/networking as one of its new strategic growth pillars, targeting opportunities across Industry 4.0, automotive and data-center applications. MCHP highlights Single Pair Ethernet as a roughly $4-billion served available market, spanning automotive, aerospace, robotics, industrial vehicles, building controls, industrial controls, sensors, actuators and vehicle networking. The company also sees billions of legacy nodes as potential replacement opportunities, giving the expanded portfolio a sizable long-term addressable market.
The launch is also well timed with improving demand in MCHP's two largest target markets for these products. In the first quarter of fiscal 2027, industrial represented 32.2% of revenues and automotive accounted for 15%. Industrial revenues increased 24.3% year over year, while automotive revenues jumped 29.3%. Industrial and automotive customers had largely completed inventory corrections, and Microchip noted that clients were placing a higher number of orders, while bookings remained strong across product lines, business units and geographies. The new devices are expected to help Microchip capture more semiconductor content as automotive and industrial networks migrate from fragmented legacy architectures toward consolidated Ethernet-based systems.
Texas Instruments' DP83TD555 targets 10BASE-T1S connectivity, while ADI's AD3300/AD3301 family brings integrated Ethernet connectivity to edge sensors and actuators.
Texas Instruments is challenging Microchip across automotive and industrial connectivity through its broad Analog and Embedded Processing portfolio, strong manufacturing capacity and growing semiconductor content per system. In the second quarter of 2026, TXN's industrial revenues increased roughly 30% year over year, while automotive revenues rose in the mid-teens. Texas Instruments' supply capabilities further intensify the challenge. The company has available clean-room space and is expanding production capacity to address rising demand.
Analog Devices poses a significant challenge through its high-performance analog, sensing, power and embedded technologies. Industrial accounted for 49% of ADI's third-quarter fiscal 2026 revenues and increased 53% year over year, led partly by automation, while automotive represented 25% of revenues and grew 16%. ADI said its higher content and share positions are driving automotive growth across next-generation ADAS, infotainment and electric powertrains. ADI is also positioning for the emergence of physical AI, including robotics and autonomous mobility.
MCHP's Share Price Performance, Valuation & Estimates
Shares of Microchip have appreciated 22% year to date, outperforming the broader Zacks Computer and Technology sector's rise of 21.8%.
The MCHP stock is trading at a premium, with a trailing price/book multiple of 6.55 compared with the Zacks Semiconductor – Analog and Mixed industry's 6.48. Microchip has a Value Score of D.
The Zacks Consensus Estimate for Microchip's fiscal 2027 earnings is currently pegged at $3.63 per share, up 15.6% over the past 30 days, suggesting 121.3% growth from fiscal 2026's reported figure.

Texas Instruments Extends Dividend Growth Streak to 23 Years with 7% Raise
Texas Instruments Incorporated (NASDAQ:TXN) has raised its quarterly dividend by 7% to $1.52 per share from $1.42, bringing the annualized payout to $6.08. The increase marks the company's 23rd consecutive year of dividend growth. The new dividend is scheduled to be paid on November 10, 2026, to shareholders of record as of October 30, subject to formal board approval.
The increase is notable because TI is raising its payout while its cash generation has improved. For the 12 months through June 2026, TI generated $8.7 billion in operating cash flow and $6.5 billion in free cash flow, while returning $5.8 billion to shareholders.
Also read: McDonald's (MCD) Achieves 'Dividend King' Status as It Raises Payout for 50 Consecutive Years
Texas Instruments Extends Dividend Growth Streak to 23 Years With 7% Raise
TI's Improving Free Cash Flow Creates More Room for Dividend Growth
The 7% increase is a stronger signal for income investors than the previous 4% raise. TI is increasing the payout while its cash generation has improved sharply. In the 12 months through June 2026, the company generated $8.67 billion in operating cash flow and $6.53 billion in free cash flow, up from $1.76 billion of free cash flow a year earlier.
That improvement matters because Texas Instruments Incorporated (NASDAQ:TXN) has been investing heavily in manufacturing capacity. Capital expenditures were $3.31 billion over the latest 12 months, down from $4.94 billion a year earlier. TI expects 2026 capital spending of $2 billion to $3 billion, suggesting the pressure from its elevated investment cycle is easing. The dividend also appears increasingly supported by free cash flow. TI paid $5.11 billion in dividends over the latest 12 months against $6.53 billion of free cash flow. That leaves a meaningful cushion, rather than requiring the company to fund the dividend primarily through borrowing or asset sales.
The 23-year record adds another layer of confidence. TI says its objective is to provide a dividend that is both sustainable and growing, and the latest increase is consistent with its stated goal of returning all free cash flow to owners over time.
Dividend Faces a Test From Its Investment Cycle
The main concern is that the dividend still consumes a large portion of free cash flow. Although the latest figures are much better, dividends of $5.11 billion compared with $6.53 billion of free cash flow leave less flexibility than the headline cash-flow growth might suggest. TI also continues to invest billions of dollars in manufacturing capacity.
The dividend yield is another consideration. The new $6.08 annualized payout translates to roughly a 2.3% yield at recent share prices, so investors are relying on continued dividend growth rather than a high current income stream.
There is also a risk that the recent improvement in free cash flow could moderate if TI's capital spending remains elevated or rises again with its expansion plans. The company says capital expenditures beyond 2026 will depend on revenue and growth expectations, so the cash available for dividends could remain sensitive to its investment cycle.
The 7% dividend increase makes the dividend case stronger than the earlier 4% increase suggested. Texas Instruments Incorporated (NASDAQ:TXN) is now growing the payout at a healthier rate while free cash flow has recovered substantially and capital spending is coming down from its peak.
The key number to watch is the relationship between free cash flow and dividends. At present, TI is generating enough free cash flow to cover the dividend with a cushion, but the payout is still consuming a significant share of that cash. For dividend investors, the next question is whether TI can sustain its improving free cash flow trend as its manufacturing investments continue.

As the artificial intelligence boom matures, choosing between high-growth processors and steady analog chips requires a careful look at Advanced Micro Devices (AMD +2.95%) and Texas Instruments (TXN +4.44%) as potential long-term investments.
Advanced Micro Devices focuses on high-performance computing for data centers and gaming, while Texas Instruments dominates the analog world with chips for industrial and automotive uses. While both operate in the same broad category, their business models and growth profiles offer very different opportunities for retail investors today.
Advanced Micro Devices designs processors and graphics chips for everything from laptops to massive data centers. Key partnerships include a strategic agreement with OpenAI to deploy advanced graphics units, alongside long-term deals with Sony (SONY +1.41%) and Microsoft (MSFT +0.92%) for gaming hardware. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business since a few large buyers drive much of the volume.
In fiscal 2025, revenue reached nearly $34.6 billion, an increase of 34% over the prior year. Net income was roughly $4.3 billion, and AMD reported a net margin of approximately 12.5% for the year. This upward trend highlights the strong demand for the company's newest products among semiconductor stocks.
As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is approximately 0.1, indicating that AMD relies very little on borrowed money. The current ratio, which measures a company's ability to pay short-term debts with current assets, is roughly 2.9. Free cash flow reached nearly $6.7 billion, though note that stock-based compensation represented roughly 21.2% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.
Texas Instruments offers a massive catalog of more than 80,000 products, focusing on analog and embedded processing. The company serves over 100,000 customers globally, primarily in the industrial and automotive markets. Because the customer base is highly diverse, with roughly half of total revenue generated by customers outside of its largest 50, the company does not rely heavily on any single buyer.
In fiscal 2025, revenue reached nearly $17.7 billion, up 13% compared to the previous year. Net income was $5 billion, resulting in a net margin of roughly 28%. In its latest annual report, filed for the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, Texas Instruments highlighted its focus on making electronics more affordable through its manufacturing scale.
Based on the December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is close to 0.9. The current ratio is approximately 4.4, suggesting the company maintains a strong cushion for its immediate financial obligations. Free cash flow for the year was nearly $2.6 billion, providing capital to support its long-term manufacturing expansion and return value to shareholders.
Advanced Micro Devices faces intense competition from Intel (INTC -0.56%) and Nvidia (NVDA +1.34%), especially following strategic partnerships between those rivals. Geopolitical risks are also present, as U.S. export controls on advanced chips to China have caused inventory charges. Additionally, the company relies heavily on TSMC (TSM +2.96%) for manufacturing and must navigate the integration of recent acquisitions like ZT Systems.
Texas Instruments must manage the cyclical nature of the chip industry, which often sees volatile demand. Because the company owns its manufacturing plants, it faces high fixed costs that are difficult to reduce during market downturns. Significant revenue comes from customers in China, making it vulnerable to trade barriers. TI is also currently in the middle of acquiring Silicon Laboratories (SLAB +0.11%).

Which stock would I buy in 2026?
Presumably, investors are paying a premium for AMD because of its strong revenue growth (Texas Instruments' growth didn't come close to AMD's last fiscal year). That said, I am more interested in each company's net margin. Using fiscal 2025 figures, TI's margin pretty handily tops AMD's full-year results. And while both companies have seen profits expand by a few percentage points over the trailing 12 months, that profitability gap has continued into this fiscal year.
As far as their actual business models, I do think AMD's fabless approach is more attractive, because it gives the company more flexibility. Texas Instruments, conversely, has to deal with the high fixed costs of owning and running its manufacturing plants.
AMD stock has absolutely exploded over the past 10 years, while Texas Instruments shares have modestly outperformed the S&P 500 over that same time frame. Past performance is no indication of future results, but it's worth taking into consideration.
All told, I like Texas Instruments better here because it appeals to the conservative side of me: It’s not crazy expensive, it has stronger profitability, and it pays a dividend yielding just over 2.1%.

PRAGUE, Oct. 1, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Zephyr Developer Summit – The Zephyr® Project, an open source project at the Linux Foundation building a secure, connected and flexible real-time operating system (RTOS) for resource-constrained devices, today announced that Texas Instruments (TI) and Infineon Technologies have upgraded to Platinum membership. Announced ahead of the Zephyr Developer Summit, co-located with Open Source Summit Europe, the expanded commitments from two leading semiconductor companies reinforce growing industry investment in Zephyr as a vendor-neutral, open source foundation for embedded development.
TI and Infineon bring longstanding technical relationships with the Zephyr community. TI has contributed to the project since its inception in 2016, providing software and board support while integrating Zephyr across its embedded portfolio. Infineon is also an active contributor and supports Zephyr across multiple embedded platforms. The move to Platinum membership will provide additional resources for the project's technical development, infrastructure and community programs.
"Ten years ago, Zephyr set out to give the embedded industry a common open source RTOS that companies could build on together," said Kate Stewart, Vice President of Dependable Embedded Systems at the Linux Foundation. "Seeing two major semiconductor companies that have contributed to Zephyr for years increase their participation is a strong sign of how far that model has come. This support gives the community more resources and makes Zephyr available to more developers building embedded products."
Since its launch, Zephyr has grown into a global ecosystem spanning a broad range of architectures, boards and embedded applications. As open source plays a growing role in embedded development, Zephyr provides a common platform where semiconductor companies, developers and product manufacturers can collaborate on shared technology. The increased engagement from TI and Infineon will help Zephyr advance its technology, hardware ecosystem and developer community as it enters its second decade.
"As a platinum-level member, Infineon is expanding its investment in the Zephyr community to help developers bring connected, resource-constrained devices to market more efficiently," said Clark Jarvis, Zephyr Governing Board Representative at Infineon. "Building on a decade of Zephyr innovation, we are committed to enabling greater software reuse and portability across our microcontroller (MCU), automotive MCU, and connectivity portfolios. This deeper engagement reflects our ambition to deliver an even better developer experience, strengthen security, and broaden hardware support throughout the Zephyr ecosystem."
"TI is committed to breaking down the barriers between hardware and software through continuous innovation. The Zephyr Project is a cornerstone of that effort," said Marian Kost, vice president and general manager of Wireless Connectivity at TI. "We are continuing our investment in open-source software and the developer community. TI wants to ensure that everyone – from a hobbyist to an engineer – can accelerate their path from concept to commercial product."
The upgraded memberships come as the Zephyr community gathers in Prague at Open Source Summit Europe to continue celebrating the project's tenth anniversary. The week opens with the Zephyr Maintainers Forum on Oct. 6, a working session where maintainers, Technical Steering Committee members and subsystem owners set the project's technical direction on release planning, security and safety support, and cross-subsystem coordination. It is followed by the Zephyr Developer Summit on Oct. 7-9, featuring more than 40 technical sessions from over 45 speakers across functional safety, security and CRA readiness, connectivity, developer tooling and testing, and real-world use cases in automotive, space and industrial applications. The summit also hosts the Zephyr Community Awards on Oct. 7, recognizing standout contributors from across the ecosystem for their work and support over the last decade.

Microchip Technology MCHP has expanded its 10BASE-T1S Single Pair Ethernet portfolio with the launch of the LAN8679 and LAN8680 PMD transceivers and the LAN8660X/1X/2X endpoint family with integrated transceivers. The products are designed for next-generation zonal architectures across automotive, industrial, robotics and aerospace and defense applications, extending Ethernet connectivity to edge nodes while reducing wiring and system complexity. The portfolio combines transceivers, endpoint functionality, power management and embedded-control capabilities, thereby supporting MCHP's broader Total System Solutions strategy. It also improves competitive prowess against the likes of Texas Instruments TXN and Analog Devices ADI.
The LAN8679 features an Open Alliance 3-Pin interface in a compact package, while the LAN8680 adds power management, wake as well as sleep control and watchdog supervision. The LAN8660X/1X/2X family integrates a transceiver into a single-chip Remote Control Protocol solution, eliminating the need for external PHY components in applications such as control systems, lighting and audio. Microchip's 10BASE-T1S multidrop architecture can connect eight or more nodes over a single bus, helping reduce wiring weight, costs and gateway requirements.

MCHP highlights Single Pair Ethernet as a roughly $4-billion served available market, spanning automotive, aerospace, robotics, industrial vehicles, building controls, industrial controls, sensors, actuators and vehicle networking. The company also sees billions of legacy nodes as potential replacement opportunities, giving the expanded portfolio a sizable long-term addressable market.
